# Large Language Models

## When, why, whether?

Large language models are better for some tasks than others. They have become very good at writing the sort of simple, short programs that are common in experimental psychology. They can be very good at finding bugs or giving you a template to build on. 

They can also be of use by acting as an expert conversation partner where you bounce ideas around, but be much less confident here. You have fewer opportunities to verify the accuracy of what they are telling you. The code you can just run.  

Whether to use an LLM depends on your goals. They are especially useful when they allow you to automate a repetitive or time consuming task that is not cognitively demanding or critical to the research goal. For instance, you have to change all the formatting from one reference type to another. You just want it done, and you don't really care how it is done. Even in this case you want to have a way of verifying the output is correct, e.g. are the references correctly formatted in the new output?. As another example: you might have trouble figuring out why your formatting is off in a document. You just want it fixed. You will be able to tell by looking if it is fixed. Then let an LLM fix it. 

If you want to learn something, then you may wish to *not* use an LLM. People who code a lot often find that there are unconventional choices made by LLMs. They may find overly complex solutions. These coders know this and can recognize it, because they can read the code and see what the LLM has done. If you don't know how to read the code yourself you may grow a mass of spaghetti that will cost you more time untangling than you thought you saved with the LLM. When you are beginning to code there is great value in learning the basic structures on your own, and then using that knowledge to bootstrap the quality of code your write later on with an LLM. 

## How to run

Use the browser interface only for quick chats that you intend to discard. It is hard to capture the output from browser chats later if you want to build or integrate them into your own knowledge database or as the starting point for a new conversation. Other tools are available that make recording and saving the output of your chats much easier. You will that below.

### Pay up

To get the state of the art models you will need to pay, however, it can be difficult to choose which model and which plan. To help with this there are several aggregators that will funnel your requests to any of a number of models. You pay one fee to the aggregator and then the aggregator passes on some of the money to the host model. You can buy one set of credits that you can easily use with multiple vendors. 

#### OpenRouter

[Openrouter](https://openrouter.ai/) is the vendor that I currently use for this purpose. An account is free to create and use. You can only use free models and then you don't have to pay at all, but I recommend buying 10.00 of credit and then you can test all the new models as they come out. For this course module you will need to create an account. You can use whatever method you prefer, but note that you can use your github account (see the icon that looks like a cat). This makes sense since you will often be using openrouter to help with your code.

To find the free models look for the "models" menu near the top right. After selecting it you can type "free" in the search bar and see the models that are free.  The small clipboard icon after each models name will allow you to copy the official model name you will need to access it later with the tools described below.

### Aider

[Aider](https://aider.chat/) allows you to invoke the AI model from your terminal. You type `aider` at your terminal and off you go. 

To use aider, which is a program, you need to install it. The aider chat website will take you to a getting started page that shows you the terminal commands you can run to install aider.

Before you begin using aider you will need to think through where to establish your first test project. Aider can run in any directory, but it assumes you are starting it in the top directory of the program project. It can look down into subdirectories, but it cannot go "up" to others. If you are just exploring create a test directory and `cd` into that before beginning. Aider will, by default, ask to create a git repository to track its changes. Say yes. This allows you to more easily revert any of the changes aider makes. If you already have a git repo allow aider to commit to it. Aider will ask. 

Since you are in the terminal your conversation appears in the terminal and commands to aider are preceded by a forwardslash (/). `/help` will get you a list of available things to do. Try starting with `/ask`. All the conversation occurs in your terminal and even the things that look like code do not get written anywhere. `/architect` will let you get aider's design ideas on a project. You can `/add` files and then ask aider to edit and fix them. For example, if you had a simple posner cuing task and now wanted to record reaction times in a csv file for each trial, you could ask aider to do that and it would, with your permission, edit your code to make the changes. To control which model aider is using you use the `/model` command to then type or paste in your choice. 

Many terminals have a history file that saves the inputs and outputs for the last N entries. You can use that to save some of your conversations or you can just copy and paste from the terminal into a document file. You don't have the breaks and blocks that can make it tedious to save a conversation from the web browser applications. 

Having trouble getting your qmd file to behave exactly as you want? Let aider take a crack at it. 

The usage guide for aider is found [here](https://aider.chat/docs/usage.html).

## Run locally

Using a LLM can mean different things. There is the training of the LLM and then there is the inference made by the LLM. The former often takes the large data centers that you hear about, but it can be done for smaller size models on work stations. You and I are unlikely to have a sufficiently capable machine. However, dowloading the trained parameters and running a model locally is very doable with higher end commercially available desktops (and some "gaming" laptops). These can be augmented with local sources to probe particular topics. You can also run them in a server mode so that you could have a user "talking" to your local model without any data crossing the internet. This gives your greater privacy, control, and reproducibility.

Running a model locally benefits from a GPU and RAM. With advances in quantization a speedy CPU helps, but is less critical. Some of the new AMD chips have integrated GPUs that are quite capable. 

Most of the use of a local model can be done with python. And in a virtuous cycle you can get an LLM to help you program the code you need.  

### LM Studio
[LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/) will give you the ability to download an app that you can then use to download all the billions of weights that make up a particular model. Start small if you have a lower spec'd laptop. After that you can converse via the app and your conversations are private and local. You can also upload up to five sources (e.g. pdfs) that will then be used to aid the model in retrieving answers pertinent to that material (a process called RAG for retrieval augmented generation).

### Ollama
[Ollama](https://ollama.com/) is an online repository of a number of very powerful models and provides the tooling for you to be able to run them locally. The [quickstart guide](https://docs.ollama.com/quickstart) provides your best starting point. 

With this software installed you can run larger models locally. Embed large collections of documents and run special inquiries and conversations with tailored prompts for particular collections. It is worth a look, but it is beyond what we will be doing in our course here.

### Using LLMs for Dynamic Research

With a model running locally you could use this in your experimental pipeline to take in user input and return model output. 

What are the mechanics we need for this? We need our model to accept input and generate output and we need a method to transfer the elements of the conversation back and forth. The first stage is to think of the components we have used so far and how we might stitch them together for this task. 

It is also a useful transitional step to work incrementally. First, maybe try to set up an interface to allow someone to talk to the model via a web interface. Then you might be able to figure out how to use [GET and POST](link) from PHP to communicate between two web servers. There are definitely better ways to do that, but it is a fairly direct starting point. If you want an additional challenge perhaps try to use the tool: [curl](https://medium.com/@kevinkoech265/curl-a-deep-dive-into-command-line-data-transfer-8361a85b177d).

# In class practice exercise

## Prerequisites

- OpenRouter account created (free at [openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai/))
- Aider installed on your system
- Basic familiarity with the terminal/command line

## Get Your OpenRouter API Key

1. Log in to [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/)
2. Navigate to "Keys" in the top menu
3. Click "Create Key" 
4. Copy your API key (you'll need it in a moment)

## Set Up Your Environment

In your terminal, set your OpenRouter API key as an environment variable:

**Use your terminal (if on Windows do this in your WSL terminal)**

```bash
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY='your-key-here'
```

There are ways to avoid having do this export directly every time, but for now we will just keep it simple and require this manual step. Note that if you bought credits then you want to keep the key confidential. Anyone with the key can access your credits. Think of the key like a password. 

## Create a Working Directory

```bash
mkdir ~/aider_tutorial
cd ~/aider_tutorial
```

## Copy the Buggy Pong Game

Copy the `pong_buggy.py` file from the course materials into your working directory.

In order for you to have something structured to play with I had an LLM create a version of Pong with two bugs. You will use aider and a model of your choosing to find the bugs and fix them. Ideally, without having to know very much about the game was even programmed.

## Launch Aider

In your terminal, from your working directory, type:

```bash
aider
```

Aider will ask if you want to create a git repository. Type `y` and press Enter. This allows you to track changes and revert if needed.

## Select a Free Model

At the aider prompt, type:

```
/model meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct:free
```

This connects you to a free model via OpenRouter. You should see confirmation that the model has been set. I have chose one example available at the time of writing. This may no longer be available. Feel free to chose any free alternative you fancy. 

##  Add the File to Aider's Context

```
/add pong_buggy.py
```

This tells aider which file you want to work with, and give aider access to make changes to that file. 

## Ask Aider to Identify Problems

Type the following at the aider prompt:

```
/ask Can you review this pong game code and identify any bugs or issues that would prevent it from working correctly?
```

**Important:** Read the response carefully. Does it identify the bugs? Does it explain them clearly?

## Request Fixes

Now type:

```
Fix the bugs you identified in the pong game code.
```

Aider will show you the proposed changes. If you agree, type `y` to accept the changes.

## Verify the Fixes

Exit aider by typing `/exit`.

Run the pong game:

```bash
python pong_buggy.py
```

Test the game:
- Use W/S keys to move the left paddle
- Use Up/Down arrow keys to move the right paddle
- Does the ball bounce correctly off both paddles?
- Does the score update correctly when the ball goes past each paddle?

## Review the Git History

```bash
git log --oneline
```

You should see commits made by aider showing what was changed.

To see the actual changes:

```bash
git diff HEAD~1
```


## The Bugs (Reference - Don't Peek!)

The file contains two bugs:

1. **Scoring bug:** When the ball goes past the right paddle, `score_a` is incremented instead of `score_b`
2. **Collision bug:** The x-coordinate check for paddle_b collision is wrong (checks `> 300` instead of `> 340`)

## Key Takeaways

- LLMs can be very effective at identifying logical errors in code
- **Always verify the output** - just because the LLM suggests it doesn't mean it's correct
- Using version control (git) with aider lets you safely experiment and revert changes
- Free models can handle many programming tasks adequately
- The `/ask` command is useful for exploration; direct commands make actual changes

## Next Steps

**Copy** your experimental program you are using for the final project to a new directory (you could also copy the qmd files and such if you want). Then `cd` to that directory and launch aider. Repeat the steps where you pick the model and add the necessary files to the aider chat. Then you can ask aider to evaluate your program and you can try to let the llm make modifications and fixes to your files.
